title: 4.1 · How a message travels (Packets, routes, protocols)
name: How a message travels (Packets, routes, protocols)
summary: Students run the Envelope Relay with a lost packet the receiver must ask for again, then learn what protocols are for in Packet Post's Rules of the Road: numbering, acknowledging, resending only the missing packet, catching damaged packets with a checksum and choosing a faster path past a busy router. One device per student.
iCan: explain what a protocol is for: numbering, acknowledging and resending packets
say how a checksum spots a damaged packet and why every router needs the same rules
materials: Envelope Relay kit: one printed picture cut into 4 numbered pieces and 4 envelopes
doNow: How does a picture get from your tablet to a friend's tablet across town? Draw it in 3 boxes. What could go wrong on the way?
plan: Explore: Envelope Relay with a lost packet, then Many Roads level 5

warmup.why: first lesson of the unit: the unit opener, the vocabulary item and today's three exit items as a pre-test; nobody is expected to know them yet, so say so before you start

do: Run the Envelope Relay with 4 numbered pieces and four student routers. Hold back envelope 3. The receiver must say what arrived (got 1, got 2, got 4) and ask the sender for piece 3 again.
Open Packet Post at Many Roads, level 5, on the projector. The packets must arrive within a hop budget: ask the class for a path that stays inside it and avoids the busy router, then send.
say: A protocol is a set of rules every computer on the network agrees on: number the packets, say got it, and ask again for anything missing.
Without the same rules everywhere, a packet from one network could not be passed on or rebuilt on another.
ask: Our receiver said got 1, got 2, got 4. What should the sender do next, and how does it know?
explore.afterAsk: Take answers until someone says resend only packet 3. Write ACK = got it on the board. That is the first rule in today's chapter, Rules of the Road.
explore.bigIdea: Protocols are the shared rules that get every packet delivered: number it, acknowledge it, resend what is missing.

play.stretch: the chapter, then Many Roads levels 5-6 with the hop budget
play.solo: one device per student; a neighbor may read the ACK cards out loud, never touch your screen
lookFors: resending every packet instead of only the missing one
keeping a duplicate packet as if it were new information
skipping the dot count on a packet that may be damaged
play.misconception: A protocol is not the road a packet takes: it is the rules both ends follow, like numbering, acknowledging and resending only the missing packet.
earlyFinishers: help a neighbor without touching their screen

discuss: What would happen with no numbers on the packets?
Why do all routers need the same rules? What would break if one used its own?
showMe: One student shows the level with the ACK cards on the projector; the class calls out which packet to resend before the student taps.

exit.sentencePrompt: What is a protocol for? Give one rule from today and what would go wrong without it.

hint 1 lists the packets that arrived

order the five rule cards and explain each in one line

unpluggedTwin.title: Envelope Relay with rules
materials: one printed picture cut into 6 numbered pieces
a dot count on each piece as a checksum
steps: Run the relay with six numbered pieces. The receiver sends an ACK card back for each piece that arrives.
Hold back one envelope. The sender waits for the missing ACK and resends only that piece.
Damage one piece: tear off a corner. The receiver counts the dots, finds the count is wrong and asks for that piece again.
Send a duplicate piece. The receiver keeps one copy and throws away the other.
Share: write the class's rules on the board in order. That list is a protocol.

subPlan: Do Now on paper, 3 minutes: how does a picture get from your tablet to a friend's tablet across town, and what could go wrong on the way? Draw it in 3 boxes.

Play Packet Post, chapter Rules of the Road, on your own for 20 minutes. Classes, then the lesson, then Play. If the game asks, the quest code is 3 2 0 0. Goal: 4 levels. No warm-up and no projector needed; playing signed out is fine.
Paper exit ticket: the half-sheet with three questions and the sentence frame. Collect it.

The warm-up is a pre-test for unit 4: nobody is expected to know the answers yet. Say so before you start.
Vocabulary beyond the five on the learn card: network, route, router, reassemble, sequence number.
One device per student at this band.

steps.body:

Big idea: Protocols are the shared rules that get every packet delivered: number it, acknowledge it, resend what is missing.

We will talk about:

- Why do all routers need the same rules? What would break if one used its own?
